item.title: Racagi death investigation findings with ODPP- Tudravu
item.description: Pita Toganivalu , Vijay Narayan · 29/09/2026 Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says the investigation into the death of Lami Police Constable Peniasi Racagi is with the Office of the DPP, with police awaiting legal advice before taking further action.
item.content:encoded:
Pita Toganivalu , Vijay Narayan · 29/09/2026

Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says the investigation into the death of Lami Police Constable Peniasi Racagi is with the Office of the DPP, with police awaiting legal advice before taking further action.

Tudravu was responding to questions on the case during the Police Remembrance Day today.

He says the Police Force understands the concerns of Racagi’s family and the general public about the progress of the investigation.

However, Tudravu says police are guided by established processes and systems.

He says questions about the early arrest made in the case are also part of the investigation process.

Constable Peniasi Racagi was murdered in Lami on the 22nd of February this year.

Police had earlier stated that their investigations focused into two avenues of the officer's death and Police involvement.

item.title: Electoral and political party amendment Bills to be debated on Thursday
item.description: The Electoral (Registration of Voters) Amendment Bill and Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Amendment Bill will be debated in Parliament on Thursday. Under the proposed Electoral (Registration of Voters) Amendment Bill 2026, a Corrupt Electoral Practices List would be established for people convicted of corrupt electoral practices.
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral (Registration of Voters) Amendment Bill and Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Amendment Bill will be debated in Parliament on Thursday.

Under the proposed Electoral (Registration of Voters) Amendment Bill 2026, a Corrupt Electoral Practices List would be established for people convicted of corrupt electoral practices.

The Supervisor of Elections would be required to place a person on the list if they have been convicted of a corrupt electoral practice within the previous four years.

A person could also be placed on the list if the Court of Disputed Returns reports during an election petition that the person is guilty of a corrupt electoral practice.

T he list would include the person’s name, voter number, residence and details of the conviction or court report.

A person convicted of a corrupt electoral practice would also be disqualified from registering on the National Register of Voters for four years.

The Supervisor of Elections would have the power to remove from the voter register anyone placed on the list or otherwise disqualified from voter registration under electoral laws.

Meanwhile, the proposed Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) (Amendment) Bill 2026 would introduce campaign expenditure limits of $300,000 for each candidate and $3 million for each political party.

The limits would apply from the first day of the campaign period until 60 days after polling day.

Income pledged or expenditure incurred outside the campaign period for use during the campaign period would also be included when calculating the limits.

Gifts given by candidates or political parties to villages or community groups as protocol to obtain permission to enter their territory would have to be declared and included in campaign expenditure .

The Bill states that such a declared gift would not constitute bribery under the Electoral Act.

Exceeding the campaign expenditure limit would be classified as a corrupt electoral practice.

Candidates would also be required to provide the Registrar with information within 60 days after polling day on the money they received, the amount and source of donations and their campaign expenditure.

The proposed amendments would also allow certain donations that are currently restricted, provided they are declared to the Registrar within 60 days after polling day.

The Registrar would be required to publish the donation declarations on the Registrar’s website.

Both Bills will be debated and voted on in Parliament on Thursday.

item.title: Tui Nayau backs GCC consultation in constitutional review
item.description: The Great Council of Chiefs’ consultation with 278 chiefs from all 14 provinces must be respected in the constitutional review process. This was highlighted by the Gone Turaga Bale na Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara who says the consultation, which represented chiefs serving about 504,609 iTaukei, was not a token exercise but a deliberate and culturally grounded process.
item.content:encoded:
The Great Council of Chiefs’ consultation with 278 chiefs from all 14 provinces must be respected in the constitutional review process.

This was highlighted by the Gone Turaga Bale na Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara who says the consultation, which represented chiefs serving about 504,609 iTaukei, was not a token exercise but a deliberate and culturally grounded process.

He says it reflected the traditional way iTaukei communities have discussed matters of great importance, with chiefs deliberating and speaking on behalf of their communities.

Ratu Tevita has given his full support to the Great Council of Chiefs and its Chairman, Ratu Viliame Seruvakula, for the consultation they led as part of the constitutional review.

He says the Great Council of Chiefs is not a partisan body and carries a responsibility to safeguard iTaukei identity, land and customs.

Ratu Tevita says dismissing the consultation could also mean dismissing the authority of chiefs, and he is urging all parties to approach the issue with care and humility.

He also acknowledges that the Constitution Review Commission’s report did not give the Great Council of Chiefs everything it had sought.

Ratu Tevita commends Ratu Viliame for accepting the outcome, saying that’s part of the process is that they accept it and are happy with it.

He says this demonstrates maturity and leadership, and is the kind of approach needed from leaders who put the interests of the country ahead of themselves.

The Tui Nayau also says the call for greater constitutional protection of iTaukei identity, land and custom is not intended to come at the expense of other communities.

He says Indo-Fijians, Rotumans, part-Europeans and all other communities who call Fiji home should be assured that iTaukei rights and the rights of all Fijians are not necessarily in opposition to their rights.

Mara says protecting Fiji’s Indigenous identity can provide a foundation for a united Fiji, while recognising and respecting the country's diversity.

He refers to the late Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara’s 1992 call for a common path towards unity that transcends race and religion and recognises that all are sons and daughters of Fiji.

Ratu Tevita says belonging does not erase distinction, but allows Fiji to embrace its different communities while preserving what makes the country unique.

A s Parliament begins debating the Constitution Review Commission’s report this week, Ratu Tevita says scrutiny of Government is an important part of a healthy democracy.

He says concerns about the inclusivity of the consultation deserve a fair hearing, but criticism should also come with constructive alternatives.

Ratu Tevita is urging members of Parliament, both Government and Opposition, to approach the debate with what he describes as the gravity and generosity of spirit the process demands.

Ratu Tevita says he stands with his people and, in doing so, stands for all of Fiji.
